existing_incident_edges.relationship: Anderson’s account becomes a named interlocutor for Chatterjee’s argument about colonial difference
existing_incident_edges.evidence_note: Chatterjee is a critic and theorist in his own right; postcolonial accounts do not simply extend Anderson. Chatterjee’s primary 1993 pp. 4–7 praise aspects of Anderson while explicitly disputing modular derivation. A new reverse critique records that productive disagreement.

existing_incident_edges.relationship: Chatterjee challenges the modular account associated with Anderson through colonial historical difference
existing_incident_edges.evidence_note: Primary pp. 4–7 formulate the objection while retaining print and language as relevant resources. The critique is not a rejection of all national imagining.

existing_incident_edges.relationship: Explains national fellowship through historically formed imagining and vernacular print markets; imagined membership does not mean falsity or personal acquaintance.
existing_incident_edges.evidence_note: Selected Introduction pp. 2–7 and complete publisher print excerpt. Limited/sovereign community and horizontal fellowship are his analytical proposals despite actual inequality. Print capitalism opens possibilities; the excerpt explicitly rejects an automatic equation of language reach with state boundaries. No citation-derived influence claim.

existing_incident_edges.relationship: Distinguishes the state’s institutional interests from the nation and investigates colonial continuities in Indonesia’s New Order.
existing_incident_edges.evidence_note: Anderson’s complete displayed 1983 author extract, full article unread. Cribb’s specifically named 2010 reading contests a simple colonial resurrection, stressing mixed historical inheritances. The relation identifies a historical research problem and disputed thesis, not an endorsed single genealogy.

existing_incident_edges.relationship: Examines how colonial census classifications, territorial maps and museums organize the space and historical ancestry available to national imagining.
existing_incident_edges.evidence_note: 1991 preface xi–xv and Census, Map, Museum opening pp. 163–167. Census/map/museum architecture is identified in the preface; census classification opening is read directly. Southeast Asian empirical scope and author’s tentative framing retained; entire map and museum sections unread. These additions are not silently dated to 1983.

existing_incident_edges.relationship: Reconsiders nationally self-contained comparisons through anticolonial and anarchist connections, circulation and communication technologies.
existing_incident_edges.evidence_note: Own later memoir paragraph explicitly reflects on an earlier nation-by-nation method, and selected Under Three Flags prologue opening follows Isabelo de los Reyes. Later self-correction and book’s original 2005 date stay distinct; no comprehensive reading of its networks or claim of equal uptake with Imagined Communities.

existing_incident_edges.relationship: Uses the fragmentary, multilingual traces of Kwee Thiam Tjing to investigate local cosmopolitanism without assuming that cosmopolitan subjects must travel widely.
existing_incident_edges.evidence_note: Anderson’s own first interview answers in Spring 2009, distinguished from Foo’s account of the 2008 talk. The project remains unfinished in this testimony. No completed biography, transparent recovery of the subject, or general endorsement of every later historical assertion in the interview.

existing_incident_edges.relationship: Partha Chatterjee’s 1993 intervention challenges Anderson’s modular derivation of colonized nationalisms and foregrounds autonomous cultural imagining in colonial Bengal.
existing_incident_edges.evidence_note: Specifically named critic, primary The Nation and Its Fragments pp. 4–7 freshly reread in rotated scan/OCR. Chatterjee acknowledges the print-capitalism insight while contesting derivative national models; material/spiritual distinction remains his historically situated claim.

existing_incident_edges.relationship: Pratt uses Anderson’s account of imagined communities to question homogeneous models of speech communities and distinguish them from unequal contact zones.
existing_incident_edges.evidence_note: Arts of the Contact Zone, Contact and Community, selected digital pp. 4–5 of the reformatted reproduction (not original journal page numbers). This is explicit analytical appropriation. Pratt does not claim Anderson believes real nations homogeneous, and this is not a reverse critique of Anderson. Broken reproduction footnote is not used as evidence.

existing_incident_edges.relationship: Greene qualifies Anderson’s account of intercolonial connections and challenges what he reads as an insufficiently lived and materially grounded account of corporate identity.
existing_incident_edges.evidence_note: Own 2019 answer explicitly accepts some mercantile links and the importance of Spanish imperial geography, but stresses competitive/local political identities and stronger transatlantic ties in other colonies. He then argues that corporate identities arise through economic practice, custom and legal culture. The suggestion that Anderson makes identity merely imaginary is Greene’s characterization, not certified here as a faithful account of Imagined Communities. Interviewer framing is distinct; Anderson 1983 original unread.

existing_incident_edges.relationship: Uses Anderson’s imagined-community framework to historicize the nation and question nationalist assumptions in immigration history.
existing_incident_edges.evidence_note: The introduction, p. 9, and the new 2014 foreword, p. xxi, explicitly invoke Anderson. The 1999 article, note 8, also cites Imagined Communities alongside Hobsbawm, Balakrishnan and Gilroy. This is a specific conceptual use, not agreement with all nationalism theory. Anderson's original book remains unread, and its editions are not conflated.

existing_incident_edges.relationship: As Breuilly explains, Colley uses Anderson’s imagined political community to treat Britain as an invented nation overlying older loyalties.
existing_incident_edges.evidence_note: Named scholarly mediation, Breuilly’s signed contribution acceptedpp.16–17 reproduces Colley’s 2003Pimlico wording and interprets the use. His qualification is essential: Colley moves from imagined community to invented nation and does not thereby adopt Anderson’s whole print-capitalism argument. Original1992and2003book bodies unread; no full-theory influence claim or claim based on citation frequency.

named_group_routes.relationship: Anderson adapts historical materialism to comparative transitions and state forms
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Editorial synthesis supported by the listed bibliography; the specific relationship remains subject to passage-level review. Anderson’s publisher describes an explicitly Marxist programme; this specifies one contributor without making Skocpol’s state analysis reducible to class.
named_group_routes.map_label: Anderson: historical materialism and divergent states

named_group_routes.relationship: Historical accounts of national formation question claims of timeless national traditions
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Editorial synthesis supported by the listed bibliography; the specific relationship remains subject to passage-level review. Hroch explicitly treats nation formation as contingent and interruptible; Smith’s qualified account of ethnic inheritances also differs from perennial nationalism.
named_group_routes.map_label: Historicizing nations without one origin model

named_group_routes.relationship: Hobsbawm and Anderson bring distinct questions about capitalism and historical construction into nationalism research
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Gellner and the entire field are not classified as Marxist. Anderson’s primary excerpt supplies a specific market/print mechanism. This is not a claim that Gellner, Smith or the whole field belongs to Marxist social history.
named_group_routes.map_label: Hobsbawm and Anderson: distinct capitalist histories

named_group_routes.relationship: invites comparison of national frameworks with cross-border historical processes
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Editorial comparison of the cited approaches, not a claim of transmission or agreement. Duara’s national/local/transnational narratives specify a project for this comparison; the publisher description does not certify all book cases or a direct Anderson influence.

named_group_routes.relationship: Gellner connects national belonging to modern mobility and a shared literate culture
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Gellner’s own book replaces Anderson as the specific reference; this does not describe every theory of nationalism. The Warwick reply supplies a primary restatement and accepts some premodern cultural continuity; Smith disputes explanatory sufficiency, not the reality of modern transformations.

named_group_routes.relationship: Ginzburg and other critics contest arguments about narrative and historical truth
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Criticism is attributed to particular participants, not to every historian or contributor to Beyond the Cultural Turn. Evans’s introduction also explicitly accepts White’s defense of scrutiny from outside the discipline. Jenkins draws on White while distinguishing their uses of discourse; criticism is not this whole entry’s position. Ginzburg 1992 body remains unchecked. Revision 1.147 adds a later witness: Perry Anderson's review of Ginzburg's Threads and Traces (LRB, 26 April 2012; WebFetch extraction) reports that "Hayden White, already criticised by Momigliano, is the King Charles's Head" of Ginzburg's defence of history "as an inquiry capable of attaining truths". Ginzburg's texts remain unread.

named_group_routes.relationship: Race as a historically made category
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Anderson (1987, abstract read) treats racial categories as cultural ascriptions whose construction cannot be taken for granted and shows government inscribing 'Chinese' and 'Chinatown' in practice and space; racial formation treats race as historically specific and produced through social and political relations. Parallel, not derivation: PhD context shows Omi or Winant cited by 1 of 172 PhDs engaging this group (and by 7 of 1303 overall).
named_group_routes.map_label: Racial formation and Canadian race history

named_group_routes.relationship: The named world-historical syntheses (Braudel, Wallerstein, Perry Anderson, Wolf) criticised as heir to Orientalist historicism: a homogenising scheme observed from a European vantage point that avoids its own relation to imperialism (1985); not a critique of every global or connected-history method
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Said's own in-period statements. 'Orientalism Reconsidered', Cultural Critique 1 (Autumn 1985), pp. 89–107, read in full (JSTOR copy). 'One of the legacies of Orientalism, and indeed one of its epistemological foundations, is historicism'; historicism 'meant that the one human history uniting humanity either culminated in or was observed from the vantage point of Europe, or the West'; out of the recuperation of what 'Eric Wolf has called people without history ... a still later disciplinary step was taken, the founding of the science of world history, whose major practitioners include Braudel, Wallerstein, Perry Anderson, and Wolf himself' (p. 101). He grants it 'greater capacity for dealing with ... the non-synchronous experiences of Europe's Other', but finds 'a fairly uniform avoidance of the relationship between European imperialism and these variously constituted, variously formed and articulated knowledges' (p. 101). 'The curious result is that the theories of accumulation on a world scale, or the capitalist world state, or lineages of absolutism depend (a) on the same displaced percipient and historicist observer who had been an Orientalist or colonial traveler three generations ago; (b) they depend also on a homogenizing and incorporating world historical scheme that assimilated non-synchronous developments, histories, cultures, and peoples to it'; 'the problem is once again historicism' (p. 102). He also rejects 're-cycling the old Marxist or world-historical rhetoric' (p. 103). In 1993 he contrasts revisionist works with 'the so-called world historians as well as the colonial Orientalists, who have tended to herd immense amounts of material under simple and all-encompassing rubrics' (Culture and Imperialism, pp. 41–42). The named historians' positions appear only as Said characterises them; no replies were looked for. The critique names practitioners mapped across several entries (Wolf on global; Wallerstein on dependency; Anderson on historicalsociology; Braudel's person entry); global is the target because he names 'the science of world history' as the object. edge_124 (post → global, Chakrabarty) stays.
named_group_routes.map_label: Said's critique of named world-historical syntheses, 1985

named_group_routes.relationship: Thompson's critique of the Nairn–Anderson theses, adopted in her account of English capitalism (1991)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Pristine Culture (1991, publisher extract, read): her preferred thesis 'is more compatible with arguments put forward by E.P. Thompson in the original debate, and less subject to his persuasive charge that Nairn-Anderson operated with an abstractly idealized model of a "Bourgeois Revolution"'. Democracy Against Capitalism ch. 2 (1995, Cambridge Core opening): anyone '(like E.P. Thompson) working somewhere in the fissures … is likely to be badly misunderstood'. 2001 (read): 'Like other Marxist historians such as E.P. Thompson, Brenner understands industrialization …'. Hirschkop (2016): 'The prominence of historians within this group (Edward Thompson and John Saville among others) was probably decisive'. Thompson's 'Peculiarities of the English' is not in the graph and unread here.

named_group_routes.relationship: The Age of… volumes (1962–1994) as a synthesis of “the capitalist world from 1789 to 1991”, praised by reviewers for range and analytical grasp and called “unashamedly Eurocentric” by Judt
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Mediated: the four volumes are unread. Guardian obituarists (2012, read in full): the series "distilled the history of the capitalist world from 1789 to 1991" and "were not conceived as a tetralogy". Judt (NYRB 1995, read in full): the trilogy's scheme "eventually became the “conventional” interpretation, now exposed to steady criticism and revision"; "though unashamedly Eurocentric, Eric Hobsbawm has a unique range" (his endnote 2 defends the European focus). Black (Historein 2003–4, p. 215): "authoritative and commanding overviews of international history from the 18th century to present". Anderson (LRB 2002) quotes Hobsbawm on Interesting Times as "world history shaping that experience". At the 2014 conference (Times Higher Education report) Mazower spoke of a "golden age of historical synthesis". Counterweights: Judt's Eurocentrism remark and the existing critiques by Guha and Chakrabarty (edges 979, 917).
named_group_routes.map_label: The Age of… synthesis, 1962–94, per reviewers

named_group_routes.relationship: The Philadelphia Negro (1899) examines a specific Black urban community; Elijah Anderson’s 2023 introduction emphasizes employment discrimination and the limits of expecting reform from informed employers.
named_group_routes.evidence_note: A named reader’s interpretation of the 1899 Philadelphia survey. This is a contribution through one study, not a claim that Du Bois founded all urban history. Isabel Eaton’s domestic-service study is separately credited; it is not treated as Du Bois’s sole-authored research.

named_group_routes.relationship: Uses Hobsbawm’s criticism of treating the nation-state as normative to frame immigration categories as historical constructions.
named_group_routes.evidence_note: The 1999 article, p. 69 and note 8, explicitly names Hobsbawm and cites the 1992 edition of Nations and Nationalism since 1780, p. 192. Anderson, Balakrishnan and Gilroy are also credited in the discussion. This is a specific appropriation, not an inference from a shared topic. The cited edition is not asserted to be the first publication, and the original remains unread.
